summary: The article reports from the set of the VR film "Through the Rift," directed by Alice Kingsleigh, and surveys how filmmaking roles are changing in virtual reality. Through interviews with a cinematographer, screenwriter, editor, sound designer and actor, it describes challenges such as the audience becoming the camera, branching scripts, guiding viewer attention, seamless stitching in post-production, spatial audio and acting for a 360-degree stage. It concludes that VR turns viewers into active participants and is building its own cinematic language.
one_line: A behind-the-scenes look at the VR film "Through the Rift" showing how directing, writing, sound, editing and acting change in virtual reality.
key_facts: The author visited the set of "Through the Rift," a VR film directed by Alice Kingsleigh, on Sunday, September 15, 2023.
Alice Kingsleigh says that in VR "the audience is the camera," so the first challenge is taking the camera out of the equation.
VR camera rigs now capture 360-degree fields of view, covering every angle of a scene.
On October 3rd, VR cinematographer Michael Robertson showed a custom-built rig; in post-production the footage is stitched into a seamless spherical world.
Screenwriter Emma Li (interviewed October 12) abandoned the three-act structure for branching narratives and said writing VR is "like writing five films at once."
Kingsleigh directed an actor in a motion capture suit and said, "You're not just directing the actors; you're directing the viewers' attention."
Directors steer the viewer's gaze with audio cues and visual signposts such as a character's movement or environmental changes.
Editor James Fisher (editing suite visit on November 1st) said VR post-production handles massive amounts of data and must produce a continuous experience with no seams.
Post-production teams also create CGI environments whose textures, lights and props must match the filmed content.
Sound designer Sofia Moreno was mixing the film's soundscape on October 29 and uses spatial audio so that a voice from behind prompts the viewer to turn around.
Lead actor David Cho said VR has "no off-camera moments" and compared it to "theater in the round but amplified."
Robertson said "We're defining the grammar of VR cinematography as we go."
The article argues viewers are no longer passive consumers but active participants who influence the narrative.
